blocks.text: A 25-year-old footballer breaks his tibia and has the leg set in plaster. Twelve hours later he is in severe pain that morphine barely touches, the shin feels hard as wood, and moving his big toe is agonising. Yet the pulse at his ankle is still present. This combination demands urgent surgery, and the reason is fixed in the anatomy of the leg's fascial compartments.

blocks.markdown: The muscles of the limbs are bundled into **fascial compartments**: groups of muscles, with their nerves and vessels, enclosed by tough deep fascia, intermuscular septa and bone. The compartments restrict how far muscle can swell, which is useful for force transmission but dangerous when pressure rises. In the leg the interosseous membrane, tibia, fibula and surrounding fascia make **four compartments**.

blocks.title: Compartment syndrome
blocks.text: A condition in which pressure within a closed fascial compartment rises high enough to reduce blood flow to the muscle and nerve inside, causing ischaemia. Because fascia does not stretch quickly, even a modest increase in volume (from bleeding or swelling) can raise pressure steeply. It is an emergency treated by opening the compartment (fasciotomy).

rows: Tibialis anterior, extensor hallucis longus, extensor digitorum longus, fibularis tertius
Branches of the posterior tibial and sural arteries
Tibialis posterior, flexor digitorum longus, flexor hallucis longus, popliteus
blocks.caption: The four compartments of the leg.

blocks.markdown: Note the actions: the anterior compartment **dorsiflexes** the ankle and extends the toes; the lateral compartment **everts** the foot; the posterior compartments **plantarflex** (the superficial group) and **invert** and flex the toes (the deep group). These actions matter in examination, because stretching a muscle that is ischaemic causes pain: passive plantarflexion stretches the anterior compartment, and passive dorsiflexion stretches the posterior compartments.

blocks.title: How raised pressure causes ischaemia
blocks.text: Tissue perfusion depends on the pressure difference between capillary blood pressure and surrounding tissue pressure. When compartment pressure rises (from bleeding after a fracture, swelling after reperfusion, crush injury, or a tight cast), the thin-walled veins and capillaries are compressed first. Venous outflow falls, pressure rises further, and arterial inflow to the capillary bed is reduced. Muscle and nerve become ischaemic although the main artery may remain open, which is why a distal pulse can still be felt. Perfusion pressure is commonly estimated as the diastolic blood pressure minus the compartment pressure.

blocks.caption: Delta pressure (perfusion pressure estimate); P is pressure in mmHg. Thresholds (a delta pressure of about 30 mmHg or less is often used as concerning) vary by guideline and institution.

blocks.title: Calculating perfusion pressure
blocks.prompt: A patient with a tibial fracture has a diastolic blood pressure of 70 mmHg and a measured anterior compartment pressure of 50 mmHg. Calculate delta pressure.

steps.text: Use delta pressure = diastolic pressure minus compartment pressure.
Compare with the commonly used cut-off of about 30 mmHg, which varies by guideline: 20 mmHg is below it, so perfusion is at risk.

blocks.answer: Delta pressure is 20 mmHg, a value that would be of concern for compartment syndrome.

blocks.markdown: **Clinical features.** The earliest and most reliable features are **pain out of proportion** to the injury and **pain on passive stretch** of the muscles in the compartment, with a tense, swollen, tender compartment. Nerve ischaemia causes **paraesthesia** and reduced sensation in the territory of the nerves in the compartment, for example numbness of the first web space of the foot (deep fibular nerve) in anterior compartment syndrome. Later features are muscle weakness or paralysis, pallor and loss of pulses. The 'six Ps' (pain, paraesthesia, pallor, paralysis, pulselessness and 'poikilothermia') are a recognised list, but pallor, paralysis and pulselessness are late signs and should not be waited for. Skeletal muscle may begin to suffer irreversible damage after about four to six hours of ischaemia, which is why speed is critical.

rows: Pain out of proportion to injury
Often the first sign; may be unrelieved by usual analgesia
Pain on passive stretch of compartment muscles
The pulse is often still present because the main artery is patent
blocks.caption: Clinical features of compartment syndrome and their timing.

blocks.title: Which compartment, which signs
blocks.prompt: A patient after a tibial fracture has pain on passive plantarflexion of the big toe and numbness of the skin in the first web space of the foot. Which compartment and nerve are involved?

steps.text: Passive plantarflexion stretches the dorsiflexors and toe extensors, which lie in the anterior compartment.
The nerve of the anterior compartment is the deep fibular nerve.
The deep fibular nerve supplies the skin of the first web space.

blocks.answer: Anterior compartment, with deep fibular nerve involvement.

blocks.title: A palpable pulse does not exclude it
blocks.text: Compartment syndrome compresses capillaries and veins at a pressure that is lower than systolic arterial pressure, so the main artery can still pulse. Waiting for the pulse to disappear means waiting too long. The diagnosis is clinical, supported by compartment pressure measurement where there is doubt, and management is urgent. First, release anything constrictive: a cast or tight dressing must be split or removed fully, down to the skin, and the limb kept at heart level (not elevated, which lowers arterial inflow further). Escalate immediately to a surgeon. If the features persist after release, or compartment pressure is high, treatment is urgent fasciotomy: surgical opening of the fascia of all affected compartments.

points: The leg has four fascial compartments (anterior, lateral, superficial posterior, deep posterior), each with its muscles, nerve and artery.
Raised pressure inside a closed compartment compresses veins and capillaries, causing ischaemia of muscle and nerve; delta pressure is diastolic pressure minus compartment pressure.
Pain out of proportion and pain on passive stretch are early warning signs; pallor, paralysis and loss of pulses are late, and these features prompt urgent fasciotomy.

questions.stem: Which nerve runs in the anterior compartment of the leg?

distractorRationale.b: The superficial fibular nerve runs in the lateral compartment.
distractorRationale.c: The tibial nerve runs in the posterior compartments.
distractorRationale.d: The sural nerve is a cutaneous nerve in the posterior leg.

questions.explanation: The deep fibular nerve accompanies the anterior tibial artery in the anterior compartment and supplies the dorsiflexors. It also supplies skin of the first web space.

questions.stem: Which muscles are in the lateral compartment of the leg?

options.text: Tibialis anterior and extensor hallucis longus
Tibialis posterior and flexor hallucis longus

distractorRationale.b: These are in the anterior compartment.
distractorRationale.c: These are in the superficial posterior compartment.
distractorRationale.d: These are in the deep posterior compartment.

questions.explanation: The lateral compartment contains fibularis longus and brevis, supplied by the superficial fibular nerve. They evert the foot.

questions.stem: Which muscle is found in the deep posterior compartment of the leg?

distractorRationale.b: Soleus is in the superficial posterior compartment.
distractorRationale.c: Extensor digitorum longus is in the anterior compartment.
distractorRationale.d: Fibularis brevis is in the lateral compartment.

questions.explanation: The deep posterior compartment contains tibialis posterior, flexor digitorum longus, flexor hallucis longus and popliteus. They are supplied by the tibial nerve.

questions.stem: A patient with a crush injury to the leg has a diastolic blood pressure of 65 mmHg and a measured compartment pressure of 41 mmHg. Using delta pressure equal to diastolic pressure minus compartment pressure, calculate the delta pressure in mmHg.
questions.explanation: Delta pressure is the diastolic blood pressure minus the compartment pressure. Subtracting 41 from 65 gives 24 mmHg, which is below the commonly used concern threshold of about 30 mmHg (thresholds vary by guideline), so the compartment needs urgent assessment.

questions.stem: Which clinical finding is typically earliest and most useful for suspecting compartment syndrome?

options.text: Pain out of proportion to the injury, with pain on passive stretch of the muscles

questions.correctOptionText: Pain out of proportion to the injury, with pain on passive stretch of the muscles

distractorRationale.b: Pulses are often present until late.
distractorRationale.d: Pallor and coldness are late signs.

questions.explanation: Pain out of proportion and pain on passive stretch are early features because the muscles are already becoming ischaemic. Pallor, paralysis and loss of pulse appear when damage is advanced.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old with a tibial fracture in a cast has worsening pain unrelieved by opioids, a tense swollen lower leg, pain on passive flexion of the big toe (passive stretch of the toe extensors) and numbness of the first web space. Pedal pulses are palpable. What is the most appropriate interpretation?

options.text: Compartment syndrome is likely; palpable pulses do not exclude it; release any constrictive cast or dressing, keep the limb at heart level and escalate urgently to a surgeon, with fasciotomy if features persist
Compartment syndrome is excluded because pulses are present
This is a normal post-fracture finding that needs only analgesia
The findings indicate a femoral nerve lesion

questions.correctOptionText: Compartment syndrome is likely; palpable pulses do not exclude it; release any constrictive cast or dressing, keep the limb at heart level and escalate urgently to a surgeon, with fasciotomy if features persist

distractorRationale.b: Pulses are usually preserved until late because the main artery is patent.
distractorRationale.c: Pain unrelieved by opioids with tense swelling is a red flag.
distractorRationale.d: The femoral nerve is not involved in the lower leg findings.

questions.explanation: Pain out of proportion, a tense compartment and pain on passive stretch with nerve symptoms point to raised compartment pressure. The pulse remains because the pressure is high enough to block capillaries and veins but lower than arterial pressure.

questions.stem: True or false: loss of the distal pulse is a reliable early sign of compartment syndrome.

distractorRationale.a: The distal pulse is usually still present in the early phase.

questions.explanation: Loss of a pulse is a late sign, because the compartment pressure needs to exceed arterial pressure to stop the pulse. Muscle and nerve are damaged well before this happens.

questions.stem: Which statement best explains how raised compartment pressure causes ischaemia?

options.text: Thin-walled veins and capillaries are compressed first, which reduces perfusion of muscle and nerve
The main artery is cut by the fascia
The muscle loses its nerve supply directly
The bone presses on the vein

questions.correctOptionText: Thin-walled veins and capillaries are compressed first, which reduces perfusion of muscle and nerve

distractorRationale.b: The fascia compresses tissue rather than cutting arteries.
distractorRationale.c: Nerve injury is caused by ischaemia, not an initial direct loss of supply.
distractorRationale.d: Bone pressure does not explain generalised ischaemia in the compartment.

questions.explanation: Venous and capillary pressures are low and are exceeded first when compartment pressure rises. The reduced outflow raises pressure further and cuts off perfusion to the muscle and nerve.

questions.stem: List the four fascial compartments of the leg with their muscles and nerves.
markingGuide: Anterior: tibialis anterior, EHL, EDL, fibularis tertius; deep fibular nerve.
Lateral: fibularis longus and brevis; superficial fibular nerve.
Superficial posterior: gastrocnemius, soleus, plantaris; tibial nerve.
Deep posterior: tibialis posterior, FDL, FHL, popliteus; tibial nerve.
Each compartment is bounded by fascia, septa and bone.
questions.explanation: Learning the compartments by function (dorsiflexors, evertors, plantarflexors, deep flexors) gives you their nerve supply too. This is the basis for predicting deficits when a compartment is injured.

questions.stem: Explain how raised compartment pressure causes ischaemia of muscle and nerve, and list the clinical features that should prompt urgent fasciotomy.
markingGuide: Fascia is inelastic, so swelling or bleeding raises pressure in a closed space.
Venous outflow and capillary perfusion are compromised first, even though the main artery may remain open.
Perfusion pressure falls (delta pressure equals diastolic pressure minus compartment pressure).
Early features: pain out of proportion, pain on passive stretch, tense swollen compartment, paraesthesia; late: paralysis, pallor, pulselessness.
Do not wait for late signs; urgent surgical escalation.
First-line steps: release constrictive casts and dressings fully to skin, keep the limb at heart level, and escalate urgently to a surgeon; fasciotomy follows if features persist or pressure is high.
questions.explanation: The key is that pressure inside a rigid space compresses the low-pressure venous and capillary system before the artery. Early recognition matters because irreversible damage can occur after several hours.
